title:
The King's
Magic Drum
description: A peaceful king owns a drum that summons a feast, and Tortoise will play any trick to make it his.

lines.text: Long ago in Calabar lived a king called Efriam Duke, who did not love war.
He owned a drum, and whenever he beat it, a feast appeared.
Fish and fufu, yams and okra, palm oil soup and palm wine, enough for everyone.
When enemies came, he did not fight. He invited them to eat.
ask: Why did the king invite his enemies?

lines.text: He feasted his people too, and even the animals, for in those days they ate together in peace.
But the drum had a rule.
If its owner ever stepped over a stick across the road, the drum would give no more food.
Three hundred Egbo men would come instead, with sticks and whips, and beat him and all his guests.
Many wanted that drum. The king would not part with it.
And the one who wanted it most was Tortoise.
One morning, Ikwor Edem, a wife of the king, took her little daughter to a spring to wash.
Above them, up a palm tree, Tortoise was cutting palm nuts.
One nut fell at the little girl's feet.
She cried for it, and her mother gave it to her.
Tortoise climbed down. That nut is mine, he said.
Ikwor Edem explained, but Tortoise was thinking of the drum.
Your wife took my food, he told the king. I want justice.
The king offered him money. Cloth. Palm kernels. Palm oil.
Tortoise said no to all of it.
At last the king said, then choose whatever you want.
Tortoise pointed straight at the drum.
To end the quarrel, the king gave it to him. But he did not tell him the rule.
ask: Why didn't the king tell him the rule?

lines.text: Tortoise carried the drum home. We will never work for food again, he told his family.
He beat the drum, and a feast covered the floor.
For three days the family ate and laughed and ate again.
Then he invited the king, the town and the animals to a grand feast.
Many laughed. Tortoise, the poorest of them all, giving a feast?
Only a few came. But the king came.
Tortoise beat the drum, and the feast appeared before them all.
The guests went home amazed. Those who stayed away swore they would come next time.
ask: What did people think of Tortoise now?

lines.text: Tortoise grew lazy and boastful, and drank too much palm wine.
One evening, walking home from his farm, he did not look where he was going.
A stick lay across the path, and he stepped right over it.
Nothing happened. He did not even notice.
The next morning, his hungry family asked for breakfast.
He beat the drum.
No food came. Three hundred Egbo men came instead, with sticks and whips.
They beat Tortoise and his whole family.
Tortoise was furious. But he did not blame himself.
If I must be beaten, he thought, so must those who laughed at me.
He invited everyone to another grand feast.
This time the whole town came, and every animal, eager not to miss out.
The king and his wives stayed home. Tortoise had sent his own family away.
ask: Why did the king stay away?

lines.text: When every guest was inside, the doors were fastened.
Tortoise beat the drum, and slipped beneath a bench.
The Egbo men burst in with their sticks and whips.
The guests ran, but there was nowhere to run.
Only Leopard escaped, leaping clean over the compound wall.
At last Tortoise opened the doors and beat the drum a special way, and the Egbo men vanished.
The guests limped home, bruised and very angry.
So the next morning, Tortoise took the drum back to the king.
Take it back, he said, and give me farms or cloth instead.
The king would not trade. But he pitied Tortoise, and gave him a magic fufu tree.
It gave fresh fufu and soup every day. But they could take from it only once a day, never twice.
ask: What was the fufu tree's rule?

lines.text: Each morning Tortoise and his wife filled their calabashes, and the family had plenty.
But one son wanted to know where the food came from.
Tortoise would not say. If the children find it, said their mother, they will spoil it.
So the boy filled a calabash with ashes and hid it in his father's bag, over a small hole.
As Tortoise walked, a thin trail of ash fell behind him.
The boy followed the trail, watched from the bushes, and said nothing.
The next day, after his father had taken the food, the boy led his brothers to the tree, and they took more.
ask: What did the boys do wrong?

lines.text: The next morning, the tree was gone.
Thick bush had grown up overnight. All Tortoise could see were prickly tie-tie palms.
He asked his family who had broken the rule. Nobody answered.
So he led them there. You broke the rule, he said, so here we must live.
And that, the old people say, is why the tortoise lives beneath the prickly tie-tie palms.
ask: Why do tortoises live under palms?
